topic: Change of Basis: Seeing the World Through Different Eyes

outline.topic: Change of Basis: Seeing the World Through Different Eyes

sections.title: Prerequisite Check: The Standard Home
sections.content: Briefly review that a 'Basis' is a set of building blocks (vectors) used to reach any point in space. Focus on the Standard Basis vectors i=(1,0) and j=(0,1). Visualize a character, 'Bob', standing on a standard square grid.
sections.example: Bob wants to reach point (3, 2). He takes 3 steps along the i-axis and 2 steps along the j-axis. This is his 'language'.

sections.title: The Perspective Shift: Enter the Robot
sections.content: Introduce a new character, 'Z-4 the Robot', who is rotated 45 degrees. Z-4 has his own basis vectors, B1 and B2, which are diagonal relative to Bob's grid. Explain that while they look at the same physical point, they use different numbers to describe it.
sections.example: A gold star is placed in the room. Bob says it's at (1, 1). Z-4, using his diagonal axes, says it's just '1 unit forward' on his primary axis (1, 0) in his language.

sections.title: The Bridge: The Transition Matrix (P)
sections.content: Define the Change of Basis Matrix (P) as a 'translator'. To build P, we express Z-4's basis vectors using Bob's coordinates. Each column of the matrix P is one of Z-4’s basis vectors written in Bob’s language.
sections.example: If Z-4's first basis vector B1 is (1, 1) in Bob's world and B2 is (-1, 1), the matrix P = [[1, -1], [1, 1]]. This matrix is the dictionary between them.

sections.title: The Calculation: Translating Coordinates
sections.content: Introduce the core formula: [x]_Bob = P * [x]_Z-4. Explain that multiplying Z-4's coordinates by P 'stretches and rotates' them back into Bob's standard grid view. Use a split-screen animation showing the vector moving from the tilted grid to the square grid.
sections.example: If Z-4 says a point is at (1, 0) in his world, we multiply P by [1, 0] to get Bob's coordinates: [[1, -1], [1, 1]] * [1, 0] = (1, 1). It matches!

sections.title: Inverse Thinking: Bob to Z-4
sections.content: What if Bob wants to talk to Z-4? Introduce the Inverse Matrix (P⁻¹). Explain that if P takes us from Z-4 to Bob, P⁻¹ takes us from Bob back to Z-4. Visualize the grid 'un-warping'.
sections.example: Bob has a point (0, 2). He uses P⁻¹ to tell Z-4 that the point is actually at (1, 1) in Z-4's coordinate system.

sections.title: Visual Summary & Application
sections.content: Summarize the flow: Basis -> Transition Matrix -> Coordinate Transformation. Mention real-world applications like computer graphics (camera angles) and data compression (changing basis to find patterns).
sections.example: Think of a video game camera: as the camera rotates, the 'basis' of the screen changes, but the 3D world stays the same. Change of basis math keeps the player aligned with the world.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite Check: The Standard Home
lecture_lines: A basis is a set of building blocks.
Meet Bob. He uses unit vectors i and j.
To reach (3, 2), he takes 5 total steps.
animations: Display a standard square grid #333333 on a black background #000000.
Animate unit vectors i (blue #0000FF) and j (red #FF0000) at the origin.
Show Bob moving 3 units along i then 2 along j to (3,2).

storyboard.title: The Perspective Shift: Enter the Robot
lecture_lines: Meet Z-4. His world is tilted 45 degrees.
He sees the same point using different basis vectors.
His coordinates describe the same location in his language.
animations: Introduce Z-4 #00FF00 with tilted basis vectors B1 #00FF00 and B2 #FFFF00.
Place a gold star #FFD700 at coordinates (1,1) on Bob's grid.
Highlight that the star is at (1,0) on Z-4's tilted grid.

storyboard.title: The Bridge: The Transition Matrix (P)
lecture_lines: We need a translator between Bob and Z-4.
The transition matrix P acts as our dictionary.
Each column describes Z-4's vectors in Bob's view.
For Z-4, P encodes his diagonal basis vectors.
This matrix maps Z-4's coordinates back to Bob's.
animations: Show Bob's grid with Z-4's diagonal basis vectors B1 and B2.
Label B1 as (1, 1) and B2 as (-1, 1) in Bob's system.
Construct matrix P #FFFFFF using B1 and B2 as columns.
Color the first column #00FF00 and the second column #FFFF00.
Add the label 'Transition Matrix' above matrix P in #FFFFFF.

storyboard.title: The Calculation: Translating Coordinates
lecture_lines: Bob's coordinates equal P times Z-4's coordinates.
Multiplying by P rotates and stretches the vectors.
If Z-4 says (1, 0), Bob calculates (1, 1).
The math bridges two different perspectives perfectly.
The tilted grid now aligns with Bob's grid.
animations: Display the transformation formula [x]_Bob = P * [x]_Z-4 in #FFFFFF.
Show the vector [1, 0] from Z-4's coordinate system.
Perform the matrix multiplication P * [1, 0] on screen.
Show the resulting vector [1, 1] appearing on Bob's grid.
Animate the grid warping from Z-4's tilted view to Bob's square.

storyboard.title: Inverse Thinking: Bob to Z-4
lecture_lines: To go from Bob to Z-4, use P inverse.
This inverse matrix un-warps Bob's standard grid.
Bob's (0, 2) translates to (1, 1) for Z-4.
animations: Display the inverse formula [x]_Z-4 = P⁻¹ * [x]_Bob in #FFFFFF.
Show the matrix P⁻¹ #FFFFFF next to the formula.
Highlight a point at (0, 2) on Bob's square grid.
Perform the multiplication P⁻¹ * [0, 2] to get (1, 1).
Morph the square grid into Z-4's tilted grid, showing the point at (1, 1).

storyboard.title: Visual Summary & Application
lecture_lines: Basis, Matrix, Transformation: that is the core flow.
This math powers camera rotations in video games.
Change of basis helps find patterns in complex data.
animations: Show a flow diagram: Basis -> Matrix P -> Transformation.
Animate a 2D camera icon rotating to show a basis change.
Show Bob and Z-4 together at the gold star's location.
